Sure. I think the only people that argue for a strictly literal meaning are people who are thinking of a narrow legal context in which the literal meaning gives a person power over others or a way out of a particular circumstance.

Proscriptive meaning and context define the descriptive meaning. What this means is that the true meaning of a given construction is dependent upon the two variables given. Namely, its agreed upon meaning (We do not use "Blue" to mean "Green"), the context which can modify that meaning, and the result of that evaluation. Ordinarily however, and on the whole, people do use words with semantic accuracy. We're surprisingly good at it. Most of us, anyway. If it were true that most words are used incorrectly, then there wouldn't exist the concept of shared meaning (implying you are incorrect in your assumption).

So if one earnestly wishes to define things in the proscriptive use in the case of a constitution, and one fallaciously believes a constitution is inherently more perfect in its original semantic context, then one simultaneously must become a linguist and a historian. When people argue about what something in law "means" they never truly are earnest - they only wish to present what they wish it to mean. Otherwise a lexicon of comparative analysis of a given phraseology would necessarily be conducted requiring whole reference libraries of literary reference from that same era.
